results.title: Surrogate data - Wikipedia
results.content: # Surrogate data. **Surrogate data**, sometimes known as **analogous data**, usually refers to time series data that is produced using well-defined (linear) models like ARMA processes that reproduce various statistical properties like the autocorrelation structure of a measured data set. The resulting surrogate data can then for example be used for testing for non-linear structure in the empirical data; this is called surrogate data testing. Surrogate or analogous data also refers to data used to supplement available data from which a mathematical model is built. Surrogate data is used in environmental and laboratory settings, when study data from one source is used in estimation of characteristics of another source. Surrogate data may be used in forecasting. Use of surrogate data may enable a model to account for patterns not seen in historical data. Another use of surrogate data is to test models for non-linearity. The term surrogate data testing refers to algorithms used to analyze models in this way. These tests typically involve generating data, whereas surrogate data in general can be produced or gathered in many ways. One method of surrogate data is to find a source with similar conditions or parameters, and use those data in modeling. Another method is to focus on patterns of the underlying system, and to search for a similar pattern in related data sources (for example, patterns in other related species or environmental areas). Rather than using existing data from a separate source, surrogate data may be generated through statistical processes, which may involve random data generation using constraints of the model or system. 1. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** ***d*** Kaefer, Paul E. results.title: Using surrogate goals to deflect threats – Center on Long-Term Risk
results.content: To avoid worst-case outcomes resulting from the execution of such threats, I suggest that agents add a “meaningless” surrogate goal to their utility function. The hope is that Bob’s threats are deflected to this new goal, assuming that Alice’s new utility function U’ = U + V puts sufficient weight on preventing the sphere (represented by V). Alice’s new utility function still includes the initial goal, though, so she continues to react to threats against the initial goal. The surrogate goal does not help in this case, but the result is at least *not worse* than what would happen by default (without utility function modification). To successfully deflect threats to the surrogate goal, Alice needs to be able to *credibly* broadcast that she now cares most about this. This is a nontrivial problem, which is exacerbated by the fact that after modifying, Alice has strong incentives to keep her surrogate goal secret – after all, leaking the information that she cares about preventing spheres of platinum might lead to threats! Unfortunately, this punishment would be directed at the initial goal rather than the surrogate goal, since this is what could deter Alice at the point where she considers modifying her utility function. Suppose they also modify their utility function to defuse threats, choosing different (unrelated) surrogate goals. Also, similar to the above point, it may be more effective to threaten the different agents individually, so this fails to achieve the goal of deflecting threats to the surrogate goal *under all circumstances*. This follows a pattern which we’ve encountered several times in this post: threats against the surrogate goal should be as similar as possible, in terms of their feasibility as a function of empirical circumstances, to threats against the initial goal. If the best policy for maximizing utility function U is to act like a U+V maximizer for certain inputs – specifically, to take threats against the surrogate goal V seriously – then the UDT agent will simply do so. The agent may also want to remove the surrogate goal from its utility function (to avoid threats against it).

results.title: What is a surrogate pair in Unicode? - Quora
results.content: Well, there are a huge amount of charsets, although most only cover a small amount of characters (like ISO-8859-16==Latin2, a char==byte encoding for Eastern Europe to use, which only covers 256 of the possible Unicode characters, the others being converted to these, losing information). Well, there are a huge amount of charsets, although most only cover a small amount of characters (like ISO-8859-16==Latin2, a char==byte encoding for Eastern Europe to use, which only covers 256 of the possible Unicode characters, the others being converted to these, losing information). UTF16 means that pretty much all characters (but not exactly all) fit into single 16-bit integers; some of these are reserved as surrogate pairs to allow for code points above 65536, that is, all the planes instead of just the first one. There are 17 planes of 65536 characters each, most of them unused (the first one is called "Basic Multilingual Plane" and contains most of the normal characters, along with the surrogate pair characters which must only appear in UTF-16, in other encodings they are actually invalid characters, while the last one is the private use plane which cannot be allocated by the Unicode consortium for other characters; the "Apple" logo in macs have a codepoint in this range). A surrogate pair is the UTF-16 encoding mechanism used to represent Unicode code points outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP) — i.e., code points from U+10000 to U+10FFFF — by using two 16‑bit code units. A surrogate pair is the UTF-16 encoding mechanism used to represent Unicode code points outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP) — i.e., code points from U+10000 to U+10FFFF — by using two 16‑bit code units. + String length measured in UTF-16 code units differs from count of Unicode characters (grapheme clusters) or code points; many languages/APIs report UTF-16 code unit length (e.g., Java, JavaScript). Summary: A surrogate pair is a two-16-bit-code-unit representation in UTF-16 that encodes one Unicode code point above U+FFFF, using one high surrogate (U+D800–U+DBFF) and one low surrogate (U+DC00–U+DFFF); correct formation and handling are essential when manipulating UTF-16 strings. While ASCII only uses one byte too represent each character, Unicode supports up to 4 bytes for each character.
